Senses.Explanation: To revile buddhas and curse patriarchs is a named act of verbal attack on the tradition’s highest figures; records use it as conduct, answer, prediction, appraisal, and self-description. Yangqi Fanghui uses a close rebuke-graph variant in a hall saying. Zhenjing Kewen applies the exact expression to Deshan; Yulin Tongxiu imagines withdrawing to a solitary peak to do it; and Guishan Lingyou predicts that Deshan will live on a solitary peak and do it. Later public questions receive it as an answer, Baoning Renyong includes it among acts that make a great buddha-work, and Zhenjing both questions what fault lies in Deshan’s conduct and says he himself will go do it. Approval, criticism, prediction, and quotation change stance, not the named act.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 適來哭，如今為甚却笑？師云：適來哭，如今笑
ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X79/X79n1557.xml). Essential Compendium of the United Lamp (聯燈會要): Baizhang Huaihai. The full-case proof distinguishes this actor from nearby respondents, questioners, and section subjects.
ClaimAnchors.ClaimText: 適來哭，如今為甚却笑？師云：適來哭，如今笑

Senses.Explanation: An audible ‘ha-ha’ laugh is assigned to the person who laughs, often closing or turning a public encounter. It is sometimes followed by speech and sometimes serves as the whole turn. The exact phrase occurs 1,829 times in 305 files representing 300 independent works. The records preserve its range without assigning one fixed motive to it. Baizhang Huaihai laughs after a colleague asks why he had just cried and answers only, “Earlier I cried; now I laugh” . Zhaozhou Congshen laughs during an exchange and then repeats Hanshan's cry, “Heaven! Heaven!” . Jinniu Heshang dances with the rice tub, laughs loudly, and calls the assembly to eat . After an unnamed member of Baizhang's assembly reports returning to eat when he heard the meal drum, Baizhang laughs. Xiangshan Yunliang laughs after a pause and asks, “Laugh at what?” . Yuanwu Keqin laughs and then calls his own address speech about a dream where there is no dream and an affair where none exists. Dahui Zonggao laughs after an unnamed questioner answers by saying farewell and immediately tests the next entrant about that response. Zen preserves the laugh as a public-interview speaker-turn and teaching-seat action rather than reducing it to an editorial report about emotion.

Senses.Explanation: Worldly toil: literally, dust and toil, and concretely the wear, bustle, and entanglement of ordinary affairs and responsive thought. The compound occurs 1,353 times in 275 allowlisted texts. Yunmen Wenyan says worldly toil is unbroken; Zhenjing Kewen says its myriad affairs are empty; and Dahui Zonggao says there is no worldly toil to avoid. Yuanhu Miaoyong answers a complaint about the toil and commotion of the world by asking who is the worldly toil and who is the one rejecting it. Dufeng Benshan calls a quiet, easeful condition only a temporary rest from worldly toil and warns against recognizing it as final. Wuyi Yuanlai pairs dwelling in dust with leaving dust and speaks of leaving the world amid worldly toil. Yunwai Ze similarly says one may dwell in worldly toil without being invaded by it. The records therefore retain the ordinary burden while testing avoidance, temporary quiet, and non-invasion; they do not make the compound a hidden name for awakening.

SearchAliases: mote after mote, land after land
Zen every mote and every land
Senses.Explanation: Across 205 occurrences in 116 allowlisted texts, Chan masters pair it with “each thing and each particular” (物物頭頭), say that every mote and land “fully displays” (全彰), and place it in public addresses as the range of an action or disclosure. One address says, “every mote and every land once manifested awe-inspiring light; each thing and each particular fully displayed the true eye” (塵塵剎剎，曾現威光。物物頭頭，全彰正眼). Another gives the compact parallel, “each thing and each particular—the whole body; every mote and every land—the great function” (物物頭頭全身，塵塵剎剎大用). The phrase is also made a test: “if you understand, every mote and every land; if you do not, a kick to the head” (若也會得，塵塵剎剎；若也不會，當頭一蹋). The corpus thus bends a cosmological distributive into recurring teaching-seat language for an all-pervading range; this entry makes no claim beyond those deployments.
